Driesch’s early theoretical writings were a critical mechanist’s attempt to reconcile the mechanist’s view of the organism as a machine with the organism’s apparent ability to adapt to changing circumstances, a view that had been developed by the German biologist Ernst Haeckel (1834–1919), and that Driesch, by introducing the concept of prospective potency, had been the first to formulate a theory of development that could explain how the organism could be a machine while still being adaptive and
The main takeaway from our work is that
Driesch’s early theoretical views were in line with the critical mechanistic approach of Wilhelm Roux, and that they were not at all incompatible with a materialist view of life.

Driesch’s theoretical writings, in particular Analytische Theorie, are not just a historical curiosity, but contain a rich and original set of insights, some of which have been rediscovered only recently (see below).

Driesch’s theory of development is not only a precursor to the current understanding of development, but it is also a precursor to the theory of evolution by natural selection, and that Driesch was the first to propose the theory of natural selection in a way that could be tested experimentally.
